REL-312.name: Shared State Checked Before an await and Updated After It
REL-312.question: Does this async function read or test shared state, then await, and afterwards write or rely on that state as if nothing could have changed it in between?

any: a cache, map, flag or field is tested (missing, not started, under a limit), an await follows, and the code then sets or uses it without testing again, so two overlapping calls both pass
a value read from shared state before an await is written back after it, such as total = total + await f()
javascript: a module-level variable, this.x or a closed-over let is read before await and assigned after it in a handler that can run again before it finishes
python: self.x or a module global is checked, an await follows, and it is then updated with no asyncio.Lock around the whole sequence
rust: a lock guard is released before .await and the value read under it is written back after locking again, without reading it again

any: the state is local to this call and no other task can reach it
no await lies between the check and the update, or an async lock or queue serialises the callers
the pending promise or future itself is stored before the first await, so later callers share it

distinguish_from.CWE-367: the state checked is a file or another external resource, not memory shared between tasks

REL-313.name: Async Function or Throwing Callback Inside a Promise Executor
REL-313.question: Does this function build a promise whose executor can fail in a way that neither rejects the promise nor reaches a handler?

javascript: new Promise(async (resolve, reject) => { ... }) where an await inside can reject, leaving the outer promise pending for ever
a throw inside a callback nested in the executor, such as in setTimeout, an event listener or a Node-style callback, with no call to reject
an error argument of a callback inside the executor is ignored and only resolve is ever called
the executor is synchronous and every failure path calls reject
the awaited work is wrapped in try/catch that calls reject, or the function is simply async and returns the awaited value
util.promisify or a promise-returning API is used instead of a hand-written executor

distinguish_from.REL-214: a promise is created and nobody awaits or handles it, with no executor at fault

REL-314.name: Completion Callback or Resolver Called Twice or Skipped on Some Path
REL-314.question: Can this function call its completion callback, next, resolve or reject more than once, or leave by some path without calling it at all?

javascript: if (err) callback(err); with no return, so execution continues and the callback is called again further down
a callback or next() called inside a loop or in both a try block and its catch
a branch, early return or caught error after which neither the callback nor resolve or reject is called, so the caller waits for ever
an Express-style handler that both sends a response and calls next(), or sends two responses
every path ends in exactly one return callback(...), next(...), resolve(...) or reject(...)
the callback is a listener meant to fire repeatedly, such as an event or stream data handler
a once-style wrapper or a done flag guards the call

distinguish_from.REL-313: the fault is an async or throwing promise executor, not the count of calls

REL-315.name: try Block Around Work Whose Error Arrives Asynchronously
REL-315.question: Does this function wrap a call in try and catch although the failure it means to handle is raised later, outside the try block?

javascript: try { setTimeout(() => risky(), 0) } catch, or a try around registering an event listener or Node-style callback that throws later
try { promiseCall().then(...) } catch or try { asyncFn() } catch with no await, so a rejection bypasses the catch
python: try around threading.Thread(...).start(), executor.submit(...), loop.call_soon(...) or asyncio.create_task(...), with the except meant for errors inside the started work
try around a call that only builds a generator or coroutine, whose body runs after the try has ended

javascript: the call is awaited inside the try, or the callback has its own try/catch or .catch handler
the catch is only for synchronous failures of the scheduling call itself
python: the future, task or thread result is awaited or fetched with result() inside the try
the generator is iterated inside the try

distinguish_from.REL-308: a promise is returned from inside try without await
distinguish_from.REL-297: no try is present; a background task's error is simply never fetched

REL-316.name: Writes Queued Without Waiting for the Sink to Drain
REL-316.question: Does this function write to a stream, socket or queue in a loop without waiting when the receiver falls behind, so pending data builds up in memory?

javascript: stream.write(...), res.write(...) or socket.send(...) called in a loop with the boolean result ignored and no wait for the drain event
a data handler that writes each chunk onward without pause and resume, pipe or pipeline
WebSocket send in a loop with no check of bufferedAmount
python: asyncio writer.write(...) in a loop with no await writer.drain()
queue.put_nowait or an unbounded asyncio.Queue or queue.Queue filled by a producer faster than its consumer, with no maxsize

javascript: pipe, pipeline or for await is used, or the loop waits for drain when write returns false
a small fixed number of writes
python: await writer.drain() follows the writes, or the queue has a maxsize and put is awaited
a small fixed number of writes

distinguish_from.CWE-770: resources are allocated per request without a cap, rather than writes outrunning a slow receiver

REL-317.name: select! or Timeout Dropping a Future With Work Half Done
REL-317.question: Does this function race futures so that the loser is dropped part-way through an operation that cannot safely be abandoned?

rust: tokio::select! in a loop with a branch such as read_exact, read_to_end, read_line, write_all or a multi-step async fn, built afresh each iteration, so bytes already read or written are lost when another branch wins
tokio::time::timeout or futures::select around a future that holds partly applied state, such as a message half sent or a transaction half done
a future dropped by select! after it took an item from a channel or lock but before using it
every branch is documented cancellation safe, such as recv on an mpsc channel, or the future is created once, pinned outside the loop and polled by reference
the dropped work is idempotent or its partial progress is kept in state outside the future

distinguish_from.REL-311: the future is never polled at all

REL-318.name: Lock Guard Released at Once by Binding It to an Underscore
REL-318.question: Does this function take a lock but drop the guard straight away, so the code it was meant to protect runs unlocked?

rust: let _ = mutex.lock(); or let _ = rwlock.write(); followed by code that touches the protected data
mutex.lock().unwrap(); as a bare statement used as if it held the lock for the rest of the block
a guard created inside an inner block or a temporary expression that ends before the access it should cover
the guard is bound to a name such as _guard or guard and lives until the end of the critical section
the lock is taken only to read or copy one value within the same expression

distinguish_from.REL-242: the guard is held too long, across an await or re-entrant call, instead of dropped too early

REL-319.name: Process Exit or Return Before Pending Work or Buffered Output Completes
REL-319.question: Does this function end the process, the runtime or itself while work it started or output it buffered may still be unfinished, so that work is silently lost?

javascript: process.exit() called right after console.log, a stream write, a logger call or an un-awaited promise, so pending output or requests are cut off
a serverless or request handler that returns or responds before a promise it started has settled
python: work handed to a daemon thread, or a task from create_task, with the main function returning or calling sys.exit or os._exit before it finishes
os._exit or a kill after writing to a buffered file or stdout with no flush
rust: main or a runtime block returns while tokio::spawn or thread::spawn work is not joined, or std::process::exit skips destructors that flush a BufWriter
c: _exit, abort or quick_exit after buffered stdio output with no fflush, or main returning while detached threads still write results

any: started work is awaited, joined or drained before the exit, and buffers are flushed or closed
the abandoned work is deliberately best-effort, such as telemetry, and the code says so

distinguish_from.REL-294: the objection is that library or handler code ends the whole process at all, not that pending work is lost
distinguish_from.REL-297: the background work runs to completion but its error is never looked at

REL-320.name: Fixed Sleep Used to Wait for Another Task or External State
REL-320.question: Does this function pause for a fixed time in the hope that another thread, process or service will have finished by then, instead of waiting on a signal of completion?

any: a sleep or delay of a fixed length placed after starting a thread, process, server or request and before using its result, with no check that the result is ready
a sleep added before a retry, read or assertion with a comment or name suggesting it lets something settle, start up or propagate
javascript: await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 500)) before reading state another task writes

any: the code waits on a join, future, condition variable, event, channel, health check or readiness probe
the sleep is inside a polling loop that tests the awaited condition and has a deadline
the delay is the function's purpose, such as rate limiting, backoff between retries or animation timing

distinguish_from.PERF-021: a loop polls with no sleep at all and wastes CPU
